lessons.title: Values, types and input
lessons.prepare: Approved Python 3 editor, paper for type sorting and a saved Week 1 badge script.

slides.title: Values, types and input
slides.notes: Explain that learners will choose a type by meaning, convert suitable input and justify a prediction. This is formative practice.
body: Unit 1 · Week 2 · Lesson 1
Choose a type that fits what a value means.

slides.title: Retrieval: the badge program
slides.notes: Allow one minute without notes, then compare with a partner. Expected quantity is input, quantity × 3 is processing, print displays output. input returns text and int converts suitable text. If learners think input returns a number, demonstrate type(input(...)) with 4 before continuing.
body: Without notes, name the badge program’s input.
Which line calculates the cost?
Why did we use int(input(...))?
Compare with a partner, then correct your explanation.

slides.title: Four useful Python types
slides.notes: Model the first row, then learners suggest another example for each type. A count is int, a measurement can be float, an identifier stays str and a two-state value is bool. Capitalisation matters in True and False. Avoid presenting float as an exact decimal representation.

slides.title: The same digits can mean different things
slides.notes: Think aloud: the first line joins strings and the second adds integers. Expected 123 then 15. Learners predict first, run, then annotate which values change type. input always returns str here. int("12.5") raises ValueError while float("12.5") gives 12.5. Demonstrate the failure in a separate interpreter, explaining that error handling comes later.
body: Predict the first two outputs before running.
Explain why they differ.

slides.title: A type depends on its purpose
slides.notes: Two minutes individually choosing types, three comparing, then share justifications. Expected locker label str, student count int, temperature float and consent flag bool. A number-looking identifier does not require arithmetic. Keep a label such as 0042 as a string to preserve its zeros. Support: supply the four type names. Stretch: explain why converting an identifier may lose information.
body: Choose a type for each value and explain why.
Locker label "0042" and student count 28.
Temperature 18.5 and permission True.
Compare with a partner before changing your answers.

slides.title: A measurement calculator
slides.notes: Learners predict for length 2.5 and width 4: Area: 10.0, then run using suitable numeric input. Driver runs and navigator explains conversions, then swap for 3 and 2: 6.0. Each learner records predictions and results. Support: identify which lines read, calculate and display. Stretch: explain why int(input(...)) would reject the text 2.5.
body: Predict for length 2.5 and width 4.
Run, compare and explain one conversion.
slides.code:
length = float(input("Length: "))
width = float(input("Width: "))
area = length * width
print(f"Area: {area}")

slides.title: Which conversion fits?
slides.notes: Collect A/B/C responses simultaneously. Correct B preserves 0042. A produces 42 and C produces 42.0. If several choose A, revisit identifier versus quantity and recheck a phone extension with a leading zero. Do not imply bool("False") parses a Boolean word; non-empty strings are truthy, which is beyond today’s input task.
body: An identifier must keep its leading zeros.
Choose alone, then justify your answer.
What information could conversion remove?

slides.title: Exit ticket: a type and a reason
slides.notes: Expected str for 0075, float for 1.75 metres, int for 6 items and bool for an on/off flag. "6" + "2" gives "62" and int("6") + 2 gives 8. Collect without partner help. Use errors to group a brief type/conversion refresher next lesson.
body: Choose types for label "0075" and length 1.75.
Choose types for a count and an on/off flag.
Predict "6" + "2" and int("6") + 2.
Give a reason for one choice.

lessons.title: Operators and changing values
lessons.prepare: Python editor, paper trace tables and counters or a sketch of objects in groups.

slides.title: Operators and changing values
slides.notes: Link to Week 1 calculations. Success means predict arithmetic, explain precedence, trace an update and interpret quotient/remainder for non-negative quantities.
body: Unit 1 · Week 2 · Lesson 2
Predict calculations before you run them.

slides.title: Retrieval: text or number?
slides.notes: Expected "45", 9 and float for a fractional measurement. Give one minute individually, then compare explanations. If string concatenation still causes confusion, show the two expressions side by side before introducing additional operators.
body: Predict "4" + "5" without running it.
Predict int("4") + 5.
Which type suits a measurement with a fraction?
Explain one answer to a partner.

slides.title: Arithmetic operators
slides.notes: Model the first four operators briefly, then use counters for 17 objects packed four per group. / returns a float for these operands, so 17 / 4 is 4.25. // floors the quotient, giving 4, and % gives remainder 1. Restrict grouping tasks to non-negative integers and positive group sizes. A zero divisor raises ZeroDivisionError.

slides.title: Order changes the result
slides.notes: Model multiplication before addition for 2 + 3 * 4 = 14. Parentheses first gives (2 + 3) * 4 = 20. Learners then independently predict 18 - 6 / 3 = 16.0. Multiplication and division share precedence and evaluate left to right here. Check all responses before moving on. Support: underline the first operation.
body: Predict 18 - 6 / 3 and show your working.
Compare the first operation with a partner.

slides.title: Assignment updates the stored value
slides.notes: Model count = 4, then the right side count + 1 uses the old 4 and assigns 5, then multiplying by 2 assigns 10. Learners annotate the value after each line and predict print output 10. Repeat independently from count 7, giving 7, 8, 16. = assigns and == compares. Python assignment is not a mathematical claim that count equals count plus one.
body: Write the value of count after each assignment.
Try again with a starting value of 7.
slides.code:
count = 4
count = count + 1
count = count * 2
print(count)

slides.title: Cones packed in boxes
slides.notes: For 29 cones and six per box, expected full boxes 4 and remaining 5. Learners complete and run the code, then swap driver/navigator roles for tests 0, 6 and 7. Expected (0,0), (1,0), (1,1). Each learner keeps a test record. Support: give the operator meanings. Stretch: verify full_boxes * BOX_SIZE + remaining equals cones.
body: Replace each __ with the correct operator.
Predict and test for 0, 6 and 7 cones.
slides.code:
cones = 29
BOX_SIZE = 6
full_boxes = cones __ BOX_SIZE
remaining = cones __ BOX_SIZE
print(full_boxes, remaining)

slides.title: Division gives different information
slides.notes: Correct B is 2 full boxes. A gives 2.3333333333333335 and C gives remainder 2. Ask for simultaneous responses, then an explanation. If learners confuse quotient and remainder, draw two groups of six and circle the two leftovers. Recheck with 13 cones: quotient 2, remainder 1.
body: Fourteen cones go into boxes of six.
Which expression gives the number of full boxes?
Explain what each result tells you.

slides.title: Exit ticket: predict and justify
slides.notes: Expected 3 + 2 * 5 = 13, (3 + 2) * 5 = 25, 23 // 5 = 4 and 23 % 5 = 3. count = 8 then count = count + 1 gives 9. Collect working rather than output copied from Python. Use errors to revisit precedence or grouping.
body: Predict 3 + 2 * 5 and (3 + 2) * 5.
Find 23 // 5 and 23 % 5.
Trace count = 8, then count = count + 1.
Explain one answer using the operation’s meaning.

lessons.title: Binary, decimal and hexadecimal
lessons.prepare: Paper place-value grids, Python editor for checking after hand calculations.

slides.title: Binary and hexadecimal
slides.notes: Explain that the base changes notation while the value stays the same. Success means hand conversions of small non-negative integers and a second-method check.
body: Unit 1 · Week 2 · Lesson 3
Use place values to explain the same number in different bases.

slides.title: Retrieval: decimal place value
slides.notes: Expected 247 = 2 × 100 + 4 × 10 + 7 × 1. The left position is ten times the next position to the right. Let learners explain with a place-value grid. This bridge prepares doubling for binary without assuming prior binary knowledge.
body: Write 247 as hundreds, tens and ones.
Explain what the 4 contributes.
How does a position change as you move left?
Compare your explanation with a partner.

slides.title: Binary place values
slides.notes: Binary uses only 0 and 1, with each position twice the value to its right. Model 10110₂ by summing 16 + 4 + 2 = 22 decimal. Read the table from left to right. Then learners use the same headings for 11001₂: 16 + 8 + 1 = 25. Support: circle positions with 1. Ask all learners for the decimal result.

slides.title: Decimal 22 written in binary
slides.notes: Model choosing 16 from 22, leaving 6, skipping 8, choosing 4 then 2, leaving zero. Result 10110₂. Learners convert decimal 13 independently: 01101₂ or 1101₂. Leading zeros preserve value. Support: provide place headings 16,8,4,2,1. Stretch: convert 31 and explain why adding 1 needs a new position.
body: Choose place values that add to 22: 16 + 4 + 2.
Write 1 for chosen places and 0 for the others.
22 decimal becomes 10110 in binary.
Now convert decimal 13 and check by adding.

slides.title: Hexadecimal uses sixteen digits
slides.notes: Explain digits 0–9 then A=10 through F=15. For 2F hexadecimal, 2 × 16 + 15 = 47 decimal. Each hex digit maps to four bits: 2 is 0010 and F is 1111, giving 00101111. Ask pairs to explain why F is one digit rather than a variable. A bit is a binary digit, and eight bits form a byte.

slides.title: Conversion practice before Python
slides.notes: Allow seven minutes individually, three comparing working, then two using Python. Expected 11001₂ = 25; 3C₁₆ = 60 and 00111100₂; decimal 37 = 100101₂ and 25₁₆. Python bin(37), hex(37), int("100101",2), int("25",16) verify. Support: supply place grids and A–F values. Stretch: compare two methods for converting 3C. Do not accept Python output alone as hand-working evidence.
body: Convert binary 11001 to decimal.
Convert hexadecimal 3C to decimal and eight-bit binary.
Convert decimal 37 to binary and hexadecimal.
Show working, compare, then check with Python.

slides.title: Leading zeros and number bases
slides.notes: Correct B: both equal decimal 5. Leading zeros change written width, not value. A common misconception is treating the digits 101 as decimal one hundred and one. If several choose A, return to place values 4,2,1, then recheck binary 0011 versus 11. Always state the base when notation could be ambiguous.
body: Compare binary 00101 and binary 101.
A: different values     B: the same value
Choose alone and justify with place values.
How many bits form one byte?

slides.title: Exit ticket: one value, three notations
slides.notes: Expected decimal 26 is binary 11010 and hexadecimal 1A. Working: 16 + 8 + 2 and 1 × 16 + 10. A–F are hexadecimal digits for 10–15. Collect individual work. Use errors to decide whether to revisit binary positions or hexadecimal digit values in Lesson 4.
body: Write decimal 26 in binary and hexadecimal.
Show a calculation that checks each answer.
What does A mean as a hexadecimal digit?
Explain why the value stays the same.

lessons.title: Characters, code points and bytes
lessons.prepare: Python 3 editor capable of UTF-8, paper matching cards and Week 2 conversion notes.

slides.title: Characters, code points and bytes
slides.notes: Success means distinguish a character, a Unicode code point and encoded bytes. Learners revisit base conversion while investigating text representation. Keep examples to A and é to avoid implying all visible characters use exactly one code point.
body: Unit 1 · Week 2 · Lesson 4
Explain how a character connects to a number and encoded bytes.

slides.title: Retrieval: the number 65
slides.notes: Expected decimal 65 is binary 1000001 or 01000001 as eight bits, and hexadecimal 41. Working 64 + 1 and 4 × 16 + 1. Allow silent working before pairs compare. If needed, model the 64 position. Use this same value for the character A next.
body: Write decimal 65 in binary and hexadecimal.
Show place-value working for one conversion.
Compare with a partner.
What changes when we write a number in another base?

slides.title: A character and its code point
slides.notes: Explain Unicode assigns A code point 65, written U+0041 in hexadecimal. These are representations of the code-point number. UTF-8 encodes A as the single byte 41 hexadecimal. Learners match the rows to character, number and bytes. A code point identifies a character in this example; some visible characters combine multiple code points.

slides.title: Python can inspect a code point
slides.notes: Predict 65, 0b1000001, 0x41 and A, then run. ord returns a single character’s code point, chr maps a code point back to a character. bin and hex return strings with notation prefixes. Ask learners to annotate each output as number, notation or character. This code does not show encoded bytes yet.
body: Predict each line of output before running.
Which line returns the character?
slides.code:
point = ord("A")
print(point)
print(bin(point))
print(hex(point))
print(chr(point))

slides.title: An encoding determines the bytes
slides.notes: Show A: ord 65, UTF-8 hex 41, byte length 1. Show é: ord 233 (U+00E9), UTF-8 hex c3a9, byte length 2. Run the snippet with A, then change to the single precomposed é character shown. len(encoded) counts bytes. .hex() displays those bytes in hex. Explain that a code-point number is different from the encoded byte sequence. Do not generalise one visible character to one byte.
body: Predict whether é uses the same byte count as A.
Run and compare the two examples.
slides.code:
text = "é"
encoded = text.encode("utf-8")
print(ord(text))
print(encoded.hex())
print(len(encoded))

slides.title: A representation record
slides.notes: Learners complete A then swap roles for precomposed é. Expected A: code point 65/U+0041, UTF-8 41, one byte. é: 233/U+00E9, UTF-8 c3a9, two bytes. Navigator explains which column comes from ord and which from encode. Each learner records an explanation. Support: use the previous snippet. Stretch: explain why decimal 233 alone does not identify a file’s byte sequence without an encoding.

slides.title: How many bytes does a character use?
slides.notes: Correct B. é has code point 233 but uses two UTF-8 bytes c3 a9. A uses one. Collect simultaneous responses, then ask pairs to explain using the record. If several choose A, point to the code-point and encoded-byte columns and re-run len(encoded). A byte is eight bits, but an encoded character can occupy several bytes.
body: “Every Unicode character takes one byte in UTF-8.”
A: agree     B: disagree
Choose alone, then use A and é as evidence.
What information does a code point identify?

slides.title: Exit ticket: explain the distinction
slides.notes: Expected A has decimal code point 65 and U+0041, encoded as one UTF-8 byte 41. é uses two UTF-8 bytes. Unicode provides code points and UTF-8 supplies encoding rules. Learners explain in their own words and identify a check that helped. Use remaining base-conversion or encoding confusion for a short retrieval starter before Week 3 selection.
body: Explain character, code point and encoded bytes.
Give A’s code point in decimal and hexadecimal.
Use é to challenge the one-byte claim.
Which prediction or check changed your understanding?
